newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire lurches towards unpredictable end.
newsitem.headline: Zaire lurches towards unpredictable end.

text.p: LUBUMBASHI, Zaire - Zaire's civil war lurched towards an unpredictable endgame on Monday as rebel forces vowing to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko closed on the second city in the country while political clashes rocked the capital.

The copperbelt capital of Lubumbashi was braced to become the latest conquest of an advance which has met little resistance, and with his army on a roll, rebel leader Laurent Kabila arrived to cheering crowds in recently-taken Mbuji-Mayi.

But unconfirmed reports of a battle near Lubumbashi signalled that parts of the government's army may still be ready to fight for Mobutu, despite the fact some Lubumbashi units had already gone over to the rebels.
A local businessman with senior contacts in the army said a colonel told him government forces had surprised rebels outside Lubumbashi and killed many of them.
Speaking earlier on local radio, General Molamba Bin Lowa, head of the Zairean military for Shaba province, said the front line was 15 km (10 miles) away at Kilimasimba (Lion's Hill).
The general said a captured rebel told the army about 200 Kabila troops had entered from Zambia in seven trucks provided by the Zambian government.
"We can't give up. We are going to attack and we will be victorious," the general said, calling for calm and declaring a curfew in the city during the hours of darkness.

At the latest welcome for Kabila, rebel justice minister Mwenze Kongolo said capturing Mbuji-Mayi, the diamond-mining centre of Zaire, was important in money terms because it meant "we have deprived Mobutu of his power to fight us".
De Beers, the powerful cartel which controls the world diamond trade, confirmed it had already held talks with Kabila.
In rebel-controlled Kisangani, on the big bend in the Zaire River, the rebels said mineral companies were lining up to secure their position with the region's new rulers.
The new governor, Yagi Sitolo, said Kabila authorities were already collecting revenue from diamond sales.
"Before, all the money went straight into pockets," said Sitolo, referring to years of corruption in which Zaire's wealth enriched Mobutu, his family and army generals.

There was no word of compromise from secret peace talks in South Africa, which began with a unpromising standoff on Saturday between rebel demands that Mobutu quit and Mobutu's apparent determination to continue his 32-year regime.

In Kinshasa, political chaos grew as supporters of prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi battled troops using armoured cars to block a march on parliament, which is trying to oust the premier after only a week in office.

Several thousand protesters set up barricades of burning tyres in the capital's teeming shantytowns and police fired teargas to turn back about 1,000 demonstrators heading for the national assembly to stop Monday's opening session.
Lubumbashi appeared to be at the mercy of rebels advancing from three directions. Losing it without a fight would knock another pillar from under Mobutu's tottering edifice.
Residents awoke to surprise news that rebels were on the way in force from the southwest, after taking the town of Kipushi on the Zambian border before dawn.

Shops and businesses were closed and the streets emptied, but groups of cheering onlookers later formed outside one army barracks in the city where government troops tied on white headbands to signal their switch to Kabila.

"We've all changed sides. We're ready for the arrival of Kabila," said Sergeant Kafua Otamba of the 21st Brigade. "We've suffered enough in Zaire over the last 30 years. We must get rid of Mobutu. We've had no pay and we have no food."

After weeks of tense speculation, Lubumbashi's fate appeared sealed when a force of at least several hundred rebel troops swept through Kipushi just 30 km (20 miles) away and advanced along the road towards the Shaba province capital itself.

The Lubumbashi headquarters of the Gecamines mining company decided to shut up shop, pushing up cobalt prices in European trading. Sizarail, a Belgian-South African consortium which runs local railways, also packed away its communications equipment.
Airlines cancelled all flights to Lubumbashi as a precaution but in the city, cheering residents crowded around soldiers at one roadblock, applauding their decision to come over to Kabila's side.
"We are waiting for Kabila, he is our saviour," one said.
